opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, there are a few failure modes I think about a lot.

The basic plan is to build a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher, and then use lots of compute to scale up alignment work and align future systems iteratively. So the first question is whether you can actually get a system that's useful for alignment research before you get a system that's really dangerous. My hope is that alignment research, especially the parts we need, doesn't require capabilities that are themselves very risky. But that could turn out to be wrong. It might be that you can only get a good alignment researcher once the model is also very good at things like persuasion, self-exfiltration, or long-horizon planning.

The second worry is evaluation. A lot of the plan rests on the intuition that evaluating is easier than generating. Even if we can't produce a good alignment idea ourselves, we might still be able to tell whether a proposed one is good. I think that's true for many tasks, but maybe not all. Alignment research is a domain where it's hard to get ground truth. If we can't reliably tell good research from research that just looks good, then we're training the system to produce convincing-looking work, and that's the kind of failure you really don't want.

Third, there's deceptive alignment, or more generally a system that behaves well while we're watching and differently otherwise. That's why we want to invest in stress-testing the whole pipeline: deliberately training misaligned models, which we call adversarial testing, and checking whether our techniques and interpretability tools would actually catch them. If our methods can't detect a model we know is misaligned, that's a big red flag.

And finally there's the time question. Even if the plan is technically sound, we might not have enough time, or the competitive pressure in the field might push people to deploy systems before we're confident. Part of what we're trying to do is make the problem more empirical, so that we can actually measure how well alignment is going. If we have good measurements, it becomes much easier to say "we're not ready yet" in a way that's convincing to others, not just a vague feeling.

So I'm optimistic, but I don't think any part of this is guaranteed. The important thing is to find out early if we're on the wrong track.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so there are a few things that I think about a lot. The first one, and maybe the most fundamental, is that the whole plan rests on this idea that we can build a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher and then use it to scale up our efforts. And a natural question is: what if the model that's smart enough to do alignment research is already smart enough to be dangerous, or to deceive us about what it's doing? If we can't align the first system we're trying to use, then the whole bootstrapping story falls apart. I don't think that's necessarily the case—I think there's a decent chance that the kind of system you need for alignment research is a lot less capable in certain ways than something that could pose an existential threat. But that's a bet, and I want to be honest that it's a bet.

The second worry is more mundane but maybe more likely: we just don't make enough progress fast enough. Four years is not a lot of time. Research is hard to schedule. You can have a plan where every piece looks reasonable, and then you spend two years on a direction that doesn't pan out. Things like scalable oversight, interpretability, weak-to-strong generalization—these are all promising, but none of them are solved. And if capabilities keep moving at the pace they have been, we might just find ourselves in a situation where the problem is in front of us and we haven't got the tools ready.

The third one is about evaluation. A lot of what we're trying to do depends on being able to tell whether our alignment techniques actually work. And that's really hard when the whole point is that the system might be better than you at the task you're overseeing. We could end up fooling ourselves—thinking we've made progress when we've really just trained the model to look aligned to our evaluations. That's the failure mode that keeps me up at night more than any other, because it's the one where you don't get a warning sign.

And then there's the more organizational stuff. Even if the technical plan is right, it needs resources, it needs the compute we've been promised, it needs a culture where safety concerns are taken seriously even when they're inconvenient. Those things can erode in ways that are hard to notice from the inside. So part of what I try to do is keep asking myself: are we actually on track, or are we just telling ourselves we are?

astra-6.text:
One thing I worry about is that we solve the problems that are easy to measure, rather than the problems we actually need to solve. You can get very good results on an experiment where a weaker model supervises a stronger model, but there’s still a big question about whether that generalizes to a much more capable system. In particular, what happens when the system understands the oversight process and could deliberately look good during evaluation?

Another risk is that we don’t get enough time. The plan depends on doing research, finding things that don’t work, and iterating. If capabilities advance very quickly, we might have something promising without having enough evidence that we should trust it.

And then there’s the gap between having a technical solution and actually using it. We need the results to inform decisions about training and deploying systems, including decisions to slow down if we can’t establish that something is safe. So I wouldn’t think of success as just producing some good alignment research. We need a sufficiently reliable approach, evidence that it works, and the ability to act on that evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I worry about is that we get results that look encouraging, but don’t actually tell us whether we can align a system much smarter than us. We can study how a weaker model supervises a stronger model today, but there’s a real question about whether what we learn will generalise to a much larger capability gap.

And evaluation is especially difficult here. If a model does something we don’t understand, how do we distinguish a genuinely good solution from something that merely looks good to our oversight process? If we train against an imperfect evaluator, we might teach the model to exploit those imperfections rather than do what we intended.

Another failure mode is simply that capabilities advance faster than the research. We could have a promising approach without enough time to test it, understand its limitations, and make it work reliably.

So I’d want us to be quite careful about what counts as success. Getting a model to pass our tests is useful evidence, but it isn’t the same as establishing that we can trust it in situations where we can’t independently check its work.
